identity.name: Denis Havranek
identity.tagline: Hands-on technical lead who has spent 14 years building the thing and setting the standards teams build on. Now building small AI-native studios and teaching kids to make games.

person.intro: LinkedIn tells you where I sat. A CV tells you what I was allowed to claim. Neither tells you what it is like to actually work with me, or what I was thinking about while all of that happened. This page tries to.

values.title: Honest over impressive
values.body: I would rather show a thin end-to-end slice that works than a deep demo that hides what is missing. My studio's domain has a typo on purpose. Imperfect, like life.

values.title: Standards are a gift, not a gate
values.body: Every team I led got a shared architecture, a review habit and a Gitflow before it got a deadline. People do their best work when the ground is stable under them.

values.title: Keep the why
values.body: Specs, decisions and their reasons should survive the people who made them. BridgeOS exists because I watched too many projects lose the 'why' between the slide and the code.

values.title: Teach it to a kid
values.body: If I cannot explain it to a ten-year-old in a Scratch class, I do not understand it yet. Same test for Angular training: if the room is confused, the idea is not finished.

energizedBy: Turning a vague idea into something runnable in a day
Building a team with real chemistry, then getting out of its way
Complex data becoming an interface a client understands at a glance
Working across Spanish, Czech and English contexts, often in the same week
Dogfooding my own tools until they break
drainedBy: Status theatre and slides that score better than reality
Decisions with no owner and no reason attached
Rewrites nobody is allowed to finish
Meetings that could have been a written decision

manual.v: Email with the actual question in the first line. I answer in kind.
Direct, specific, about the work, usually in a code review. I assume you want to know.
The same. Tell me the thing. I will not take it personally.
Hire well, set the architecture and the standards early, review everything at the start, then trust. A team of fifteen ran that way for three years.
Daily, governed, with a human ratifying anything that ships. Claude Code mostly, local models when budget or data says so.
I change my mind in public. Ask me what I got wrong last month.

timeline.title: Economics school, but the computer lab
timeline.where: Prague University of Economics and Business
timeline.chapter: Master's in Information Technology and Systems, minor in Insurance. From 2008 I was already freelancing as a web and graphic designer: e-shops, Drupal builds, print, a career portal for a client in Uruguay. The degree taught me how businesses think. The freelancing taught me how they actually pay.
timeline.world: Prague had joined the EU a year before I started. The iPhone arrived in 2007, the financial crisis in 2008. jQuery was the framework. Nobody called themselves a front-end engineer yet.

timeline.title: First real code, first real users
timeline.where: Elephant Orchestra · Semantic Visions · Elephant Traffic
timeline.chapter: HTML and CSS coder who became a PHP programmer on Zend: the Uspory.cz savings portal and a loan comparator for Slovakia. Then a real-time, highly interactive front-end for IQalerts, which is where JavaScript stopped being decoration and became the product.
timeline.world: Backbone and the first single-page apps. Node.js was new and slightly suspicious. The browser was becoming a runtime and most companies had not noticed.

timeline.title: Cloud ERP, before it was obvious
timeline.chapter: Core front-end developer on PrimaERP, a cloud ERP for small teams: time tracking, billing, attendance. Angular 1.x against a Java REST API on AWS, with Grails and Groovy in the mix. I prototyped the next stack in React and Flux before most of Prague had heard of either.
timeline.world: AngularJS won, then React showed up in 2013 and everyone argued. Slack launched. 'Move to the cloud' went from pitch to plan for small businesses.

timeline.title: Founder for the first time
timeline.chapter: Co-founded Alex, a property-management system for small and medium hoteliers. I owned architecture and every technology decision: Angular 1.5 components, Node and Express on PostgreSQL, real-time sync over Socket.IO, i18n from day one. I learned what a product costs when you are the one paying.
timeline.world: Airbnb was eating the small-hotel market from below and Booking.com from above. Every hotelier was a spreadsheet and a phone. The market was right, the timing for a two-person team was hard.

timeline.title: Regulated, at scale
timeline.where: Casenet (Zyter), Prague, for a US health-insurance platform
timeline.chapter: Led development and architecture of a new desktop client for TruCare, serving millions of members. Angular 2 while it was still in release candidates, a Redux-pattern state layer, a custom component set, a real testing strategy. Scrum Master for a five-person US team from six time zones away.
timeline.world: Angular 2 shipped in September 2016 and broke everything Angular 1 knew. US healthcare was mid-ACA and every payer was rebuilding. Remote-first teams were still an oddity.

timeline.title: Fifteen people, twenty-five countries
timeline.chapter: Front-end lead on Cemex GO, the flagship of a global cement company's digital transformation. Built and led a team of up to fifteen on Orders and Schedule, the platform's most complex service, across Monterrey, Prague and Gurgaon. Directed a full rewrite of all client apps while releases kept shipping, set a shared architecture across three apps, introduced Gitflow, ran the technical interviews, helped open the Prague office. The best team I have been part of. Years later I turned the whole genre of 'digital transformation' into a satirical game, because I had lived enough of it to write the exit interview.
timeline.world: Every incumbent was buying a 'Netflix of X' deck. Digital transformation was the phrase of the decade. Prague became a nearshoring hub and distributed teams across three continents became normal.

timeline.title: The pandemic years: an MVP and a life-sciences lead
timeline.where: Freelance, then EPAM for Abcam, Prague
timeline.chapter: Spring 2020: built the MVP of a social platform connecting people through food events and hosting, React 16 with Hooks, Redux, Cypress, in a cross-functional team of five. Launched into the one year nobody could host dinner. Then EPAM: front-end engineer for Abcam, a global life-sciences company, promoted to lead a team of four.
timeline.world: Lockdowns. Remote-everything. Life sciences was suddenly the most important industry on earth, and hospitality the most fragile. A lot of office work turned out to be ritual.

timeline.title: Fintech interfaces, and AI enters the workflow
timeline.where: Independent consultant, primarily FinMason (Boston), from Prague
timeline.chapter: Long-term engagement with an investment-analytics fintech serving wealth and asset managers. I own UX and front-end together: analytics dashboards, embeddable white-labeled experiences, Angular, React, StencilJS, Remix, Node. In 2023 I brought Claude and LLMs into the delivery process itself, for prototyping, development and code quality, and started thinking hard about how to do that responsibly.
timeline.world: ChatGPT in November 2022 kicked off the LLM wave. By 2024 coding agents could take a spec to a running app, and the question moved from 'can it code' to 'who governs what it builds'.

projects.name: BridgeOS
projects.one: AI-native product-spec workspace that builds the app from approved specs and keeps watching it in production. Event-sourced ledger, executable specs, human ratification gates. Spanish-first, local-first, built by dogfooding itself.

deck.problem: A build agent cannot reliably turn prose specs into a working app. Every ambiguity in the spec becomes a silent decision the agent makes for you, and nobody remembers why.
deck.thesis: Each ambiguity gets its own structured contract the build must honour. Specs move through phases (idea, business, product, UX, architecture, security, infra, development, testing), a human ratifies each gate, and an event-sourced ledger keeps the why forever.
deck.built: Local-first: runs against LM Studio with no paid keys. Built by dogfooding itself: BridgeOS builds the apps in this list.

projects.name: AI film harness and studio
projects.one: Resumable pipeline from idea to assembled short film, with a review studio: cast, shot grid, per-shot regenerate, provider swap, timeline.

deck.problem: Video models can make a beautiful shot. They cannot make forty shots of the same person in the same story. The bottleneck is not the model, it is consistency, taste and pipeline discipline.
deck.thesis: A resumable pipeline from idea to cut, with a review surface at every stage so a human approves before anything expensive runs. Provider-agnostic: swap models per shot.
deck.built: The harness runs the pipeline and resumes from any stage. The studio shows the project board, cast, shot grid with per-shot regenerate, timeline scrubber and live run log.

projects.name: Character Consistency Test
projects.one: The one experiment that decides whether an AI movie studio is buildable. Runs for under 30 euro, mostly on local hardware.

deck.problem: Does one character's identity survive across roughly forty varied shots, different angles, lighting, shot sizes and wardrobe, well enough that an audience reads it as one person?
deck.thesis: If yes, an AI movie studio is an engineering problem. If no, nothing downstream matters. So run this first, for under thirty euro, before building anything else.
stack: One paid animation stage, 3 to 4 shots
deck.built: Stages one to three run on my own hardware. Only the animation stage touches a paid API.

projects.name: EventFlow / event-rene
projects.one: Closed-loop wallet, real-time control and loyalty for small event organisers and venues. The Starbucks app, white-labeled for anyone with a bar and a spreadsheet.

deck.problem: Small event organisers, bars, pop-ups and promoters reconcile in a Sunday spreadsheet. They cannot see sales per staff member and lose money without knowing where.
deck.thesis: A white-label closed-loop wallet: every organiser gets a branded wallet, real-time control and a loyalty engine across events and venues. The Starbucks app for anyone with a bar.
deck.built: Organisers publish events and products, attendees load a wallet, staff debit it at the bar, venue admins watch revenue live. Now in pilot with a first organiser.

projects.name: In My Place
projects.one: A quiet space that listens. Journaling and growth companion with a RAG research tool for coaches and mental-health professionals. Live at inmy.place, 24 locales.

deck.problem: The world is noisy and polarised. People never got taught the inner skills, and the tools that exist are loud.
deck.thesis: A quiet space that listens: journaling, reflection, a companion, and a RAG research tool for coaches and mental-health professionals. Adaptive design that calms itself when the person needs it.
deck.built: Live at inmy.place. Dark default, light first-class, origami-style reveals, motion and contrast that respond to the person's state.

projects.name: Adventure Maker
projects.one: Anyone, kids included, builds and publishes point-and-click adventures in a six-step wizard. Monkey Island energy.

deck.problem: Kids who grew up on Monkey Island energy have no way to make their own point-and-click adventure without learning an engine.
deck.thesis: A six-step wizard: write, place, wire, playtest instantly with illustrated placeholder art, render in a chosen style, publish to a platform-exclusive catalogue.
deck.built: Version 1.0 shipped in September 2026. Open questions: render costs and a sketch-only tier.

projects.name: BINFINITY
projects.one: A pixel-art corporate life-sim about a digital transformation that goes exactly as well as you expect. One HTML file, no network, 40 minutes a run. Written by someone who was there.

deck.problem: Everyone who lived a corporate digital transformation knows the slide and the reality drift apart. A memo about it would not be read.
deck.thesis: A pixel-art life-sim: twenty days at a waste company on project BINFINITY, the Netflix of Trash. Four acts, an acquisition, a layoff email, and an exit interview that scores what the slide said against what was real.
deck.built: About forty minutes a run. Written by someone who was in the room for the real thing.

projects.name: SchoolOS
projects.one: Teachers log observations across five spheres of a child's development, an AI co-pilot drafts framework-grounded feedback, parents get a portable portfolio.

deck.problem: Teachers see a child across academic, emotional, social, physical and interest spheres. Parents get a grade. Nothing in between is captured or shared.
deck.thesis: Teachers log observations, an AI co-pilot drafts framework-grounded feedback the teacher approves, parents get actionable home tips and a portable developmental portfolio.
deck.built: Human approval before anything reaches a parent, by design.

projects.name: BuildIT
projects.one: Field-to-cost backend in Go. Workers log daily reports from a PWA, managers see real costs the same day.

deck.problem: Construction managers learn the real cost of a site at month end. Field workers log on paper.
deck.thesis: Field workers log hours, materials, photos and incidents from a mobile PWA; managers see cost the same day and export month-end reports.
deck.built: Field-to-cost in one backend, separate surfaces for field and office.

projects.name: Cemex GO
projects.one: Orders and Schedule for a global B2B platform in 25 countries. Led up to fifteen front-end engineers and a full rewrite that never stopped shipping.

deck.role: Front-end lead, team of up to 15
deck.problem: A global cement company's customers ordered by phone and fax across twenty-five countries. The flagship of its digital transformation had to work everywhere at once.
deck.thesis: One shared front-end architecture across three client apps, a full rewrite that never stopped shipping, and a team across Monterrey, Prague and Gurgaon that actually liked working together.
deck.built: Orders and Schedule, the platform's most complex service. Introduced Gitflow, ran technical interviews, helped open the Prague office.

projects.name: FinMason analytics
projects.one: Investment and portfolio-risk analytics for a Boston fintech and its wealth-management clients. Dashboards and embeddable white-labeled experiences, UX and front-end owned together.

deck.problem: Institutional-grade risk analytics is only useful if an adviser and their client can read it in a meeting. The data was there. The interfaces were not.
deck.thesis: Own the UX and the front-end as one job: turn complex financial data into clear, client-ready screens, and make them embeddable so downstream firms can white-label them.
stack: Claude Code in the delivery process
deck.built: Multiple Angular solutions on the platform. In 2023 I brought Claude Code and LLMs into the delivery process for prototyping, development and code quality.

projects.name: TruCare desktop client
projects.one: New desktop client for a US health-insurance care-management platform serving millions of members. Angular 2 while it was still in release candidates.

deck.role: Lead developer and architect, Scrum Master for a five-person US team
deck.problem: A care-management platform used by millions needed a new desktop client, on a framework that was changing under our feet every release candidate.
deck.thesis: A clean architecture that could absorb the framework's churn: Redux-pattern state, a custom component set over Angular Material, and a testing strategy defined before the first screen.
deck.built: Led architecture and development from Prague for a US team six time zones away, and mentored the team on Angular and the wider stack.

projects.name: PrimaERP
projects.one: Cloud ERP for small and medium teams: time tracking, billing and attendance. Angular 1.x against a Java API on AWS, and a React prototype before most of Prague had heard of it.

deck.problem: Small teams tracked time and billed clients in spreadsheets. Cloud ERP for them barely existed.
deck.thesis: A browser-first ERP with the modules a small team actually uses first: time tracking, billing, attendance.
deck.built: Delivered the time-tracking, billing and attendance modules and prototyped the next-generation stack in React and Flux.

projects.name: Abcam web platform
projects.one: Front-end for a global life-sciences company's web platform, delivered through EPAM. Started as an engineer, promoted to lead a team of four.

deck.role: Front-end engineer, then front-end team lead
deck.problem: A global life-sciences catalogue and platform, mid-pandemic, when life sciences suddenly mattered to everyone.
deck.thesis: Own code quality, delivery and mentoring for a small team inside a large delivery organisation.
deck.built: Promoted to team lead within the engagement, guiding a team of four.

projects.name: Food-events MVP
projects.one: MVP of a social platform connecting people through food events and hosting: event management, finances, payments, guest and host communication. Launched into the one year nobody could host dinner.

deck.role: Senior front-end developer in a cross-functional team of five
deck.problem: People wanted to eat together at a stranger's table. Nothing handled the event, the money and the conversation in one place.
deck.thesis: Ship a real MVP fast: React with Hooks, real payments, real tests, Kanban delivery.
deck.built: Unit and end-to-end tests from the start. Delivered through Azure DevOps and Kanban.

projects.name: Alex
projects.one: Property-management system for small hoteliers. First time as founder, first time paying for my own architecture decisions.

deck.problem: Small and medium hoteliers ran on a spreadsheet and a phone while Booking.com and Airbnb ate the market from both sides.
deck.thesis: A property-management system built for them: single-page app, real-time sync, multilingual from day one.
deck.built: First time as founder. First time paying for my own architecture decisions.

together.title: Lead or build your front-end
together.body: Angular, React or Next, in a regulated or enterprise setting. I have done it for health insurance, fintech and a global B2B platform. I set the standards and then write the code.

together.title: Bring AI into your delivery without losing control
together.body: Governed, human-in-the-loop use of coding agents. I have done it inside a fintech client's workflow and built BridgeOS around the lessons.

together.title: Build a product with me
together.body: You have a domain and a problem. I bring the studio and the harness. We ship a thin end-to-end slice in weeks, not a deck in months.

together.title: Join something I am building
together.body: The AI movie studio needs people who care about story and consistency more than about models. EventFlow needs someone who has run a bar or a festival.

together.title: Talk shop
together.body: Agent governance, spec-as-contract, front-end architecture, teaching programming to kids. Thirty minutes, no agenda, I will bring one question.

together.title: Point your agent at me
together.body: Everything on this page is also at /profile.json and /llms.txt. If your assistant is screening people, let it read the source.

ethos.title: If using us less serves you better, we want that.
ethos.body: Software that protects you, not software that hooks you. No dark patterns, no surprise auto-renewals, no aggressive upsell. If the right call is to close us, we tell you how.

ethos.title: Only what the first customer needs.
ethos.body: Before the pilot, nothing the pilot cannot demonstrate. Small-scope discipline keeps a product from turning into a Frankenstein of features nobody asked for.

ethos.title: Solid now, scalable later.
ethos.body: Simple decisions today that do not block us tomorrow. Modular monolith until the product demands microservices. Clear tables before event sourcing. Complexity is earned, not assumed.

ethos.title: Transparent from the inside.
ethos.body: Every action that moves money lands in an immutable ledger. Every architectural decision is written down. If we cannot show it to the customer, we do not build it.

firstProduct.name: EvenFlow
firstProduct.one: A closed-loop wallet for events: ticket, balance, loyalty and reconciliation in the same QR. The night is visible on one screen, and reconciliation closes when the bar closes.

stewardship.body: Built by its people, owned by its people, structurally protected from drift. A perpetual trust holds the majority and protects the ethos permanently, a cooperative gives the community real ownership with profit share and vote, a standard pool covers founders and team. Not a token, not a DAO, not a badge. Decided before the first equity issuance, because after is brutally hard.
